Table Answers

Most-Watched Titles by Period
To better understand Netflix’s viewing numbers, I identified the most watched title in each reporting period and calculated its proportion of total viewing hours for its respecive period. This allows us to see how much of Netflix’s viewership is driven by its biggest titles and whether that share changes over time.


Show Code
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),.groups = "drop")|>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(proportion= total_hours / sum(total_hours)) |>
  slice_max(total_hours, n = 1)|>
  ungroup()|>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Most-Watched Titles by Reporting Period**")
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    total_hours= "Total Hours Viewed",
    proportion = "Share of total viewing hours"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_hours),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
  columns = proportion,
  decimals = 2
)|>
  tab_options(
    table.background.color = "black",
    table.font.color = "white",
    column_labels.background.color = "red",
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
    heading.background.color = "black",

section: 4. How Has Netflix’s Catalog Changed Over Time?
text:
4. How Has Netflix’s Catalog Changed Over Time?
With an abundance of streaming services popping up, its important to see how increased competition in the industry has affected Netflix’s catalog over time. Particularly we want to see if the number of available titles and total runtime have changed. By looking at these pieces of data, we are able to get a better picture on whether Netflix is expanding or reducing its content.


Show Table Code
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    total_runtime = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE),
    number_titles = n_distinct(title))|>
  arrange(desc(period))|>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**NETFLIX**"),
    subtitle = "How Has Netflix's Catalog Changed Over Time?"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    total_runtime = "Total Runtime",
    number_titles = "Number of Titles"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_runtime, number_titles),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
   tab_options(
    table.background.color = "black",
    table.font.color = "white",
    column_labels.background.color = "red",
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
    heading.background.color = "black",
    heading.title.font.size = px(40)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "red", weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
  )|>
  tab_source_note(
  source_note = md(
    "**Source:** Netflix, *What We Watched* engagement reports (2023–2026)."
  )
)

Popular Netflix titles in terms of viewership across all periods
Given the enourmous catalog of Netflix, its important to investigate what people consistently enjoy watching. Perhaps these pieces of info can could help Netflix determine which types of content are worth maintaining and invest in over the long term.


Show Code
TITLE_HOURS <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(
    hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
TITLE_HOURS |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    avg_viewership = mean(hours,na.rm=TRUE),
    min_viewership = min(hours),
    sd_viewership = sd(hours,na.rm=TRUE),
    max_viewership = max(hours),
    periods = n_distinct(period,na.rm=TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
  cv = sd_viewership / avg_viewership
)|>
  relocate(max_viewership, .after = min_viewership) |>
  filter(periods == 7) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_viewership))|>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  select(-periods) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**NETFLIX**"),
    subtitle = "Top 15 Titles by Average Viewership Across All Seven Periods"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    title = "Netflix Title",
    avg_viewership = "Average Viewing Hours(Millions)",
    min_viewership = "Minimum Viewing Hours(Millions)",
    max_viewership="Maximum Viewing Hours(Millions)",
    sd_viewership = "Viewership Variability (Millions)",
    cv = "Relative Variability (CV)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
  columns = c(avg_viewership, min_viewership,
              max_viewership, sd_viewership),
  scale_by = 1/1000000,
  decimals = 1)|>
  fmt_percent(
  columns = cv,
  decimals = 1)|>
    tab_options(
    table.background.color = "black",
    table.font.color = "white",
    column_labels.background.color = "red",
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold",

To identify Netflix’s most consistent popular titles, I filtered the table to only include shows which appeared in a 7 periods, as these provide a better picture of long-term viewership in Netflix’s catalog. I also included the coefficient of variation (CV) column to compare how consistent each show’s viewership was. When looking at the data table we can see the most popular show,in terms of average viewing hours, was the Night Agent Season 1 at approximately 222 million hours,however its CV was 119.5%. On the contrary, Pablo Escobar, el patron del mal: Season 1, had a CV of only 16.8%, meaning more pepople consistently tuned in to watch the show when compared to the Night Agent, despite having a lower average number of vieing hours. These observations signify that shows with low average viewing hours can still bring in long-term value for Netflix as long as they attract a steady audience over time.


Shows vs. Movies
Most of Netflix’s catalog comes shows and movies, so its important to understand how their viewing patterns compare. By examining viewing hours and viewership share, we can get better sense on which content type play a crucial role in Netflix’s success. For this comparison, I excluded live events, as they dont fit to either category.


Show Code
NETFLIX_CLASSIFIED<-NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    content_type = case_when(
      live_event == TRUE ~ "Unknown",
      str_detect(title, "Season") ~ "Show",
      runtime > 240 ~ "Show",
      is.na(runtime) ~ "Unknown",
      TRUE ~ "Movie"))



viewing_summary<- NETFLIX_CLASSIFIED |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")|>
  group_by(period)|>
  mutate(
    proportion = total_hours / sum(total_hours))|>
  ungroup()|>
  filter(content_type != "Unknown")

viewing_summary |>
  select(period, content_type, total_hours) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,

text:

title: MINI-Project #01: What We Watched: Exploring Netflix Viewing Data
text:
3. Most-Watched Titles by Period
To better understand Netflix’s viewing numbers, I identified the most watched title in each reporting period and calculated its proportion of total viewing hours for its respecive period. This allows us to see how much of Netflix’s viewership is driven by its biggest titles and whether that share changes over time.


Show Table Code
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),.groups = "drop")|>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(proportion= total_hours / sum(total_hours)) |>
  slice_max(total_hours, n = 1)|>
  ungroup()|>
  arrange(desc(period))|>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**NETFLIX**"),
    subtitle = md('*Most-Watched Titles by Reporting Period*')
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    total_hours= "Total Hours Viewed",
    proportion = "Share of total viewing hours"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_hours),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
  columns = proportion,
  decimals = 2
)|>
  tab_options(
    table.background.color = "black",
    table.font.color = "white",
    column_labels.background.color = "red",

text:
8. Executive Memo
To: Netflix Leadership Team
From: Jeffrey Flores
Subject: Content Strategy Recommendations for 2027 and Beyond
With increasing competition in the streaming industry, Netflix must continue to find ways to attract viewers while keeping its existing audience engaged. After examining Netflix’s viewership data from 2023 through the first half of 2026, I believe the company should focus on three areas: balancing major original releases with consistently watched content, continuing to invest in TV shows, and continue to expand into live programming.
When analyzing the top 15 titles from Netflix’s catalog, I observed that high average vieweing hours didn’t necessarily mean consistent viewership. This could stem from a show having a positive word of mouth which caused it to reach such a high average view count but eventually those viewers went away, which would explain their lack of consistent viewership. Looking at the top 15 titles dataset, we saw that the Night Agent: Season 1 accumulated an average of 222.2 million viewing hours with a coefficient of variation of 119.5%. In comparison, Pablo Escobar, el patrón del mal: Season 1 averaged 136.2 million hours but had a much lower coefficient of variation of 16.8%. The Night Agent’s higher CV indicates greater fluctuations in viewership across all the periods. Pablo Escobar’s lower CV suggests steadier viewing hours. This suggests that consistent viewership can be valuable even when a title does not reach the same peaks as Netflix’s biggest hits. Netflix should continue to make and invest in productions that can maintain long-term audience engagement.
Moving onto the importance of TV shows, we saw they accounted for a much larger share of Netflix’s overall viewership. In the latest period, TV shows accounted for approximately 94.7% of total viewing hours, compared with 2.8% for movies. It’s important to note that this discrepancy can be explained by the fact that a season of a show typically has a longer runtime. Netflix should continue developing original TV series as this is where the crux of their viewership comes from. This doesn’t mean Netflix should stop producing movies, but instead put more thought into decisions on how its budget is allocated, as the data shows that TV series’s provides a greater overall contribution to Netflix’s total viewing hours than movies.
Finally, live programming has shown potential to provide Netflix with a great boost in viewers. Live events averaged approximately 1.53 million views, compared with 1.37 million for prerecorded content. These live events provide Netflix with a substantial number of viewers to their streaming service in a short time. It is a great way to attract new customers to the platform in the hopes of retaining them as long-time customers. Netflix should continue to expand into live programming, particularly through events which have demonstrated strong audience interest.
To conclude, for 2027 and beyond, I believe Netflix’s content strategy should focus on maintaining long-term engagement, further expansion into live programming, and invest in TV series (whether that be original or licensed TV shows). By combining these 3 strategies, Netflix can work on maintaining a competitive edge in the industry, attract and retain a new customer base, and keep its existing customers engaged.

ChatGPT was used to assist with R code, including data acquisition, table formatting, and website design. It was also used to explain programming concepts, troubleshoot errors, and craft ideas for the last task. The statistical analysis, interpretation of tables, and Executive Memo were written by me.
